find: On extended staging questions about structure and pace, the most common mistake is to describe what happens act by act instead of explaining how a director communicates the structural shift to an audience. For a question about the play’s turning point, for example, you should identify Act Three as the pivot and then immediately move to concrete design and performer choices that signal the change: a lighting palette shift from warm ambers to cold blue-whites, a performer’s physical energy becoming jagged rather than fluid, a soundscape losing its musical underscore and replacing it with silence. Every structural observation needs a staging consequence. Also remember the prologue: students who mention the chorus’s role in establishing dramatic irony from the opening moments tend to score more highly on playwright’s intentions questions, because they show awareness that the audience’s knowledge shapes how every scene lands.
replace: On the 20-mark set-text question, follow the role in the question rather than retelling the plot. As a performer, turn structural ideas into vocal, physical and spatial choices. As a designer, develop one design skill and explain how it supports the action in the extract and the play as a whole.
note: F2: AQA's 20-mark set-text task is answered as either a performer or a designer, not as a combined staging response.

find: The Nurse and Friar Lawrence are the play’s surrogate adults — closer to the lovers than their actual parents, and therefore more culpable when things go wrong. Shakespeare gives the Nurse almost all her dialogue in prose, which is the language of servants and comic characters in the play. The exception is Act Four, when she believes Juliet is dead: she shifts into verse. A performer’s awareness of that verse choice as a character signal — even prose-speakers resort to the formal language of grief — is the kind of dramatic analysis examiners reward.
replace: The Nurse and Friar Lawrence are the play’s surrogate adults — closer to the lovers than their actual parents, and therefore more culpable when things go wrong. The Nurse uses both prose and verse. Prose often suits her comic, conversational exchanges, while her verse in the discovery scene can sharpen the force of her grief. A performer can use these shifts in form as one clue to changes in pace and emotional pressure.
note: F3: The Nurse uses verse as well as prose before Act Four.

find: • The Nurse’s shift from prose into verse when she believes Juliet is dead is a structural signal that even the most earthy characters resort to formal language under the pressure of grief — a detail that rewards close reading in performance.
replace: • The Nurse uses prose and verse; her verse in the discovery scene can sharpen the force of grief and guide a performer’s vocal choices.
note: F3: The conclusion repeated the false claim that Act Four is the Nurse's sole use of verse.

find: On playwright’s intentions questions about themes, the trap is to describe a theme and then list evidence without explaining what Shakespeare wants the audience to feel or understand at that specific moment. The command word “analyse” means: identify the technique, explain how it works, state its effect on the audience, and make a judgement about why Shakespeare made that choice. For Romeo and Juliet, examiners note that the best answers hold fate and free will in tension rather than choosing one: the play seems to offer both simultaneously, and that is the point. In design and performer questions about themes, be concrete — a gobo of star patterns on the stage floor, a colour-coded costume scheme, a performer’s movement vocabulary that slows with age. “Dark lighting to show the theme of fate” is the response that will not progress beyond the developing band.
replace: For the 12-mark set-text question, focus on the named performer’s use of performance space and interaction in the extract. Explain specific choices and their effect on the audience; do not turn the response into a literary essay about theme alone.
note: F5: AQA's 12-mark set-text task is a performer task, not an analyse-the-playwright's-intentions question.

find: On playwright’s intentions questions that ask about context, the most common error is presenting historical information without connecting it to a staging consequence. Every piece of context you cite must earn its place by linking to a specific design or performance choice and an effect on the audience. The Elizabethan shared-light stage, the boy actor convention, the patriarchal household — none of these is a stand-alone fact; each is a prompt for a staging choice. When you write about context in extended-response questions, use the formula: “Because [context], a director might [specific staging decision] to communicate [effect on audience] because [thematic meaning].” The examiner is looking for that chain of reasoning, not the historical fact in isolation. Also note that knowing Arthur Brooke’s poem as the source is useful only when you use it to explain what Shakespeare changed and why those changes matter for staging.
replace: For the 4-mark design question, make the specified social, cultural or historical context visible in practical design details for the extract. Name materials, colour, condition, scale or positioning that suit the context, rather than adding a separate history paragraph.
note: F6: AQA's context-linked set-text task is the 4-mark design question, not a playwright's-intentions question.

find: Shakespeare does not give every character verse. The Nurse, the servants and Peter speak almost entirely in prose. This is not random: prose signals lower social status, earthiness and comedy. A performer playing the Nurse can find permission in this: the Nurse does not have to modulate her delivery to a regular beat. She can interrupt herself, trail off, repeat, speed up in excitement, slow down in self-pity — the prose form invites natural, naturalistic vocal behaviour in a way that strict verse does not.
replace: Shakespeare does not give every character verse. The Nurse uses both prose and verse. Prose often suits her comic, conversational exchanges, while verse can sharpen emotional intensity. A performer can use the form as one clue to changes in pace, breath and pressure, rather than treating it as a fixed rule of naturalistic delivery.
note: F8: The Nurse does not speak almost entirely in prose.

find: A crucial teaching moment concerns Act 4: when Juliet is feared dead, the Nurse shifts into verse. For a performer and director, this is a precise signal from Shakespeare — the intensity of grief elevates even the Nurse beyond her usual register. A lighting designer might underline this shift: the warm, comic amber that has lit the Nurse's scenes could bleed away, replaced by a cooler lighting wash of pale blue, marking the tonal shift that the change of form announces.
replace: In Act Four, Scene Five, the Nurse’s verse as she finds Juliet can heighten the force of her grief. A lighting designer might underline the emotional shift: the warm, comic amber that has lit the Nurse’s scenes could bleed away, replaced by a cooler lighting wash of pale blue.
note: F8: The discovery-scene verse is not the Nurse's sole departure from prose.

find: • Prose versus verse signals social status and emotional register — the Nurse’s shift into verse in Act 4 is a performance cue, not just a literary fact, and a good answer translates every formal choice into specific vocal, physical and design decisions.

note: F8: The conclusion repeated the false claim of a unique Act Four shift.

find: For the 12-mark question asking you to analyse the playwright’s intentions, students frequently make the mistake of writing a literary essay: “Shakespeare uses iambic pentameter to convey Romeo’s nobility.” This will not access the top band. You must link the form to a specific staging choice and a specific audience effect: what does a director DO with the verse form, and what does the audience FEEL as a result? Aim to discuss both a performer’s vocal response to the verse AND a design choice that reinforces the form at the same named moment. For the 20-mark extended staging response, examiners want breadth: performer choices AND lighting AND sound AND costume, all anchored to the same moment of the play — never drift into generalities about the whole play.
replace: For the 12-mark set-text question, explain how the named performer would use performance space and interact with the other actor in the shaded extract. Use verse only where it informs a specific vocal, physical or spatial choice.
note: F9: The 12-mark task is a performer task, not a playwright's-intentions or combined staging response.

find: The choice is not arbitrary: the Capulets are the family with social power in Verona, and warm, saturated colours read as dominant on stage.

note: F10: The Prologue presents the two households as equal in dignity.

find: The most common error on design questions is describing a ‘mood’ without naming specific elements. Writing “I would use romantic lighting” is worth very little. A strong answer names the lantern type (profile, Fresnel, birdie, flood), the colour (a specific gel colour or temperature — warm amber, cold blue-white, daylight neutral), the direction (from above, from the side, from front-of-house) and the effect on the audience at a named moment. The same applies to costume: name the fabric (brocade, cotton, leather), the colour, the silhouette and the symbolic meaning. For the 8-mark designer question, you are expected to make specific choices for one or two design disciplines, not give a general overview of the whole production. For the 20-mark response, cover all four departments but ensure each choice is concrete and justified, not merely decorative.
replace: For the 8-mark question, make specific vocal and physical choices for the named line. For the 20-mark question, develop either the performer role or one chosen design skill, as the question requires, rather than covering all departments.
note: F12: The 8-mark task is performer-focused; the 20-mark task requires one role, not all design departments.

find: Exam answers on practitioners fail when they describe the practitioner’s biography without applying the technique to a specific moment of the play. The question is always: what would a director drawing on this practitioner DO differently at this named moment? A good answer names the technique, explains what the director would do and names the effect on the audience — all three, in sequence.
replace: When using a practitioner in an exam answer, apply the technique to a specific moment of the play. Name the technique, explain the practical choice it informs and state the effect on the audience.
note: F16: AQA does not set a distinct practitioner question in its set-text question sequence.

find: Practitioner questions are where students most often describe a biography instead of making an application. Writing “Stanislavski was a Russian theatre director who founded the Moscow Art Theatre” contributes nothing to a Drama answer. What matters is: if a director applies Stanislavski’s objective method to Juliet in the tomb scene, what does the performer DO differently? What vocal and physical choices follow from having a precise, internally motivated objective? For the 20-mark extended staging response, show you know more than one approach: compare what a Stanislavskian production would do for a named moment with what a physical theatre or Brechtian production would do — and make a directorial decision, justifying your choice. That comparative judgement is what separates the top band from the second band.
replace: When a practitioner informs a set-text answer, apply the technique to a named moment rather than reciting a biography. For the 20-mark response, develop either the named performer’s role or one selected design skill, and justify choices for the extract and the play as a whole.
note: F16: AQA's 20-mark set-text task does not require a comparison of practitioners and is answered in one role.
